analysis.one_liner: Makes hospitals and doctors automatically liable for improperly denying or transferring emergency patients.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors, the bill sat in two House subcommittees and never received any vote before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill strengthened the federal "patient anti-dumping" law, which requires hospitals to screen and stabilize anyone with a medical emergency regardless of ability to pay. It would have stripped the requirement that a hospital or doctor act "knowingly and willfully" before facing Medicare penalties, so any improper denial or transfer of an emergency patient would trigger liability, and it would have held hospitals responsible for their doctors' violations. It also extended whistleblower protection to hospital employees who report violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Emergency patients — especially the uninsured and people on Medicare — gain a stronger guarantee that a hospital cannot turn them away or transfer them while unstable, because hospitals and physicians would face penalties for any violation, not just deliberate ones. Hospital employees and medical staff who report violations would gain explicit protection from retaliation. (Sources: [S2], [S3])

how_it_helps.text: Under current section 1867 of the Social Security Act (the emergency-care law passed in 1986, often called the patient anti-dumping law), penalties apply only when a hospital or physician 'knowingly and willfully, or negligently' fails to provide required screening, stabilization, or appropriate transfer. The bill strikes that intent language, making hospitals and physicians strictly liable — meaning a penalty could follow from any improper denial or transfer of a patient with an unstabilized emergency condition, even a hard-to-prove one.

The bill adds 'agency liability': a hospital would be liable for the acts and omissions of its agents and the physicians through whom it carries out its emergency-care duties, so a hospital could not escape penalties by blaming an individual doctor.

It amends the whistleblower protections to bar hospitals from penalizing a physician who refuses to authorize transferring a patient whose emergency condition has not been stabilized, and from retaliating against any hospital employee who reports a violation of the emergency-care requirements.
The bill's enforcement amendments would take effect about six months after enactment without waiting for new regulations, so protections would not be delayed by rulemaking.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and physicians bear the cost: they would face civil monetary penalties and potential exclusion from Medicare for any violation of the emergency-care rules, with no need for the government to prove they acted knowingly, and hospitals would be on the hook for their physicians' violations. Patients benefit from the stronger deterrent. (Sources: [S2], [S3])

drawbacks.text: Strict liability removes the intent requirement entirely: a hospital or physician could face penalties even where the denial or transfer involved an honest, good-faith medical judgment, which is the strongest objection to this approach — it punishes any violation rather than deliberate wrongdoing.

By making hospitals liable for their physicians' acts and omissions, the bill pushes the full weight of penalties onto hospital institutions, which critics would say could drive defensive practices in emergency departments.
The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, suggesting little appetite in the House for tightening enforcement this far, and no committee ever weighed its costs or held a hearing on it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: stronger deterrence against turning away or transferring unstable emergency patients, and protection for employees who blow the whistle. The cost falls on hospitals and physicians, who would face penalties without any showing of intent — a tradeoff the sponsor chose deliberately but which drew no support from colleagues. Because no committee or floor vote ever examined it, there is no record of how Congress judged that tradeoff; the bill simply died in subcommittee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees in February 1990, and nothing further ever happened before Congress's term ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on February 7, 1990, the day the 101st Congress's second session was getting under way, as a solo sponsor with no cosponsors.

It was referred the same day to both the House Ways and Means Committee (which handles Medicare) and the Energy and Commerce Committee, a joint referral that splits a bill between two committees and requires both to act.
Within two weeks, each committee sent the bill to its health subcommittee — Ways and Means on February 12 and Energy and Commerce on February 23, 1990 — which is where most bills stop.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed; the action record ends with those subcommittee referrals, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and physicians came out ahead: the threat of penalties for improper denial or transfer of emergency patients without proof of intent, and liability for doctors' violations, never advanced. Emergency patients gained nothing beyond the protections already in law.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 7, 1990 as its only sponsor; no colleague cosponsored it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on February 12, 1990; the subcommittee never considered it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee sharing jurisdiction over the emergency-care law
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee on February 23, 1990; the subcommittee never considered it.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no recorded opposition; the only record of support is the Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Hospitals would face strict liability — penalties for any improper denial or transfer of an emergency patient, plus liability for their physicians' violations — making the current patient anti-dumping rules much more expensive to violate. The industry's interest in avoiding those penalties runs against patients' interest in guaranteed emergency care.

Striking the 'knowingly' requirement means a physician could face Medicare penalties for any violation of the emergency-care rules, even a good-faith judgment call on transferring a patient, instead of penalties aimed at deliberate patient dumping.

The bill's whistleblower language would protect doctors who refuse to authorize unsafe transfers and any hospital employee who reports violations from retaliation — their interest lines up with patients' protection.
